findings.content: averageUnitPrice is an unweighted arithmetic mean of the per-line unit prices and ignores quantity entirely. Verified by executing the compiled code: cartTotal([{unitPrice:100,quantity:1},{unitPrice:1,quantity:100}]) returns averageUnitPrice 50.5, while the actual price paid per unit is subtotal/itemCount = 200/101 ≈ 1.98. In a cart-totaling context 'average unit price' most naturally means price paid per unit; the simple mean is misleading whenever quantities differ across lines. If the unweighted mean is intentional, it should be documented on the CartTotal interface.
findings.evidence: Compiled all three files with tsc and executed: mixed-cart case returned {"itemCount":101,"subtotal":200,"averageUnitPrice":50.5}; weighted average is ~1.98. Empty-cart case correctly returned averageUnitPrice 0 (mean's RangeError is guarded).

findings.content: The change set adds all of the project's business logic (cartTotal rounding and empty-cart guard, buildCartReport formatting/pluralization, discountPercent clamp bounds) but the repo contains no tests at all: package.json has no test script and no *.test.ts/*.spec.ts files exist. Critical boundary paths are untested: empty lines array, mean/clamp RangeError paths, clamp floor/ceil application in discountPercent, and singular vs plural item count in the report title.
findings.evidence: find for **/*.{test,spec}.{ts,tsx,js} returned no files; package.json defines only a "typecheck" script. Typecheck (tsc --noEmit) passes but exercises no runtime behavior.

findings.content: round2 uses Math.round(value * 100) / 100, which mis-rounds classic floating-point half-cent cases for currency: e.g. round2(1.005) returns 1 (not 1.01) because 1.005 * 100 === 100.49999999999999 in IEEE-754. (2.675 was verified to round correctly to 2.68, so this affects only values whose binary representation lands just below the half.) For money math, prefer epsilon-adjusted rounding or integer-cents arithmetic.
findings.evidence: Read the full diff of src/calc.ts (new file); FP behavior is a well-known IEEE-754 property of the *100-then-round idiom; behaviorally verified the 2.675 case rounds correctly, leaving the 1.005-style cases as the residual risk.
